questions.title: Multiplayer: which kind of linking should be built first?
questions.context: Research in docs/research/multiplayer.md. The plan links games over the internet by having every player's computer run every player's game, exchanging only button presses; the link cable is then emulated exactly inside each computer. That suits Emerald's cable trades, battles, Record Mixing and Berry Blender with up to 4 players. The wireless adapter (Union Room, many players) needs a different design, and a shared overworld (seeing other players walk around) is a third, per-game layer.

options.label: Cable first: trades and battles with friends
options.changes: builds the plan as filed: link hub, local two-player window, netplay core, relay server, then june plays a friend. Wireless and shared overworld stay later research

options.label: Wireless first: the Union Room
options.changes: emulate the wireless adapter and send its radio through the server; more players, each running only their own game, but an undocumented device with unmeasured timeouts: slower and riskier. The cable units wait

options.label: Shared overworld first
options.changes: other players' avatars shown in your Hoenn, no trades or battles until later; per-game hooks, designed after the Lua scripting research

questions.title: Multiplayer: where should the server run?
questions.context: Research in docs/research/multiplayer.md. Players' computers connect to a small relay server (rooms with a 6-character code, passing button presses and game states between players). If everyone connects out to a server, nobody's router needs configuring. No machine in docs/machines.md is an always-on server today.

options.label: A machine of june's that is always on
options.changes: june names the machine and how friends reach it (a forwarded port or a tunnel); free, and latency is fine for friends nearby. The relay server unit deploys there

options.label: No server: one player hosts
options.changes: the host's game is the relay, and the host forwards a port on their router (or the connection falls back to failing); nothing to keep running, but each session needs the host's setup

options.label: A small rented server (a VPS)
options.changes: always reachable, a few dollars a month, and an account somewhere; best for friends far away

answer.note: Start the relay as a separate program (later optionally built into the game). june wants it to know nothing about the game: the same server works for any game, any console. Build a quick prototype first to find out if that holds. Which always-on machine: not named yet, ask june when the relay unit needs it.

questions.title: How much may a Lua script do on your machine?
questions.context: mGBA lets a script do anything you can: read and write any file, run programs, open network connections. The Ironmon tracker uses that: when tested here it ran curl on its own to check for updates, and it runs programs to list folders, launch the Java randomizer and open web pages. Scripts are downloaded from the internet, and on the Deck you can't easily see what one does. docs/research/lua-scripting.md, Sandboxing.

options.label: Full access, as mGBA
options.changes: every script works exactly as in mGBA, Ironmon's updater and new-run automation included; a bad script can do anything you can

options.label: Limited, with a per-script full-access switch
options.changes: scripts can only touch files in their own folder and talk to this machine; Ironmon's tracking works at once, and its updater and new-run automation work once you flip its switch (remembered)

options.label: Always limited
options.changes: the safest; Ironmon's updater and new-run automation never work

questions.title: Should scripts get breakpoints and watchpoints?
questions.context: mGBA's next version (0.11, not released yet) lets scripts stop when the game runs a given address or touches a given variable. No released mGBA has it, and none of the popular scripts checked use it. Recompiled code has no place to stop between instructions, so it costs: running the game in our interpreter while one is set is exact but about 6 times slower (still 3.7 times real speed on quack; the Deck is unmeasured). Building checks into the compiled game would slow every game a little all the time. docs/research/lua-scripting.md.

options.label: Leave them out for now
options.changes: nothing to build; a script that asks gets a warning

options.label: Yes, by running interpreted while one is set
options.changes: exact, the game runs slower only while a breakpoint or watchpoint exists

options.label: Yes, built into the compiled game
options.changes: full speed while stopped-on code runs, but every game pays a small cost always and the code generator grows

questions.title: Should our Emerald build run randomized Emerald ROMs (Ironmon)?
questions.context: The Ironmon tracker, the most popular mGBA script, starts each new run by loading a freshly randomized copy of the game. Our recompiled Emerald only runs the exact ROM it was made from, and refuses anything else. A randomizer mostly changes data, not code, so most of the compiled code would still be right. docs/research/lua-scripting.md.

options.label: Keep it compiled where the code is unchanged
options.changes: check each compiled function against the new ROM when it loads and run only changed ones in the interpreter; full speed if the randomizer leaves code alone, which is to be measured

options.label: Run other ROMs fully in the interpreter
options.changes: simple, exact, about 6 times slower than compiled but still faster than real speed on a PC

options.label: Don't support it
options.changes: Ironmon's new-run feature won't work in our build; tracking a run started elsewhere still does

withdrawn.why: june asked for research first; {unit:scripting/randomized-rom-research} measures it and asks again

questions.title: What should the in-game menus be built on?
questions.context: docs/research/ui-library.md. Whatever draws the menus, the window moves from minifb to winit: minifb can't toggle fullscreen (none on Wayland, macOS or Windows) and only stretches on resize. Both spikes ran pad-only under gamescope with no added hitching.

options.label: winit + egui (OpenGL)
options.changes: Menus and the later Lua console are egui widgets, one toolkit for both; mouse and text entry built in; pad drives egui's focus through a small adapter. Binary about +5 MB, clean build about +20 s, needs an OpenGL context.

options.label: winit + hand-drawn menus
options.changes: Menus drawn into the 240x160 frame with a pixel font, pad behaviour exactly ours, smallest (about 3.9 MB) and no GPU; every widget is ours to write, and the Lua console would need its own text UI or egui added then.

options.label: stay on minifb, hand-drawn
options.changes: Least work now; no fullscreen toggle on Wayland, macOS or Windows and no real resizable window, so those stretch units can't be done as written.

answer.note: Changed by june (2026-10-24): egui yes, but SDL3 (the sdl3 crate, vhspace/sdl3-rs) instead of winit for the window and graphics layer, and for gamepads (button labels, the Deck's controller, Steam Input), replacing gilrs; egui drawn through SDL's renderer (Vulkan/Metal/D3D as SDL picks), not OpenGL. The glue from egui to the SDL renderer may be ours to write. Audio (cpal or SDL's) is the implementer's call, say why. egui's look is ours to style; june has no opinion on egui details. Accessibility through AccessKit (AT-SPI on Linux) is wanted later, not now.

questions.title: Structured code: interpret resumes, or keep a second body?
questions.context: Structured Rust can only start at a function's entry, but after an IRQ or frame end every function on the stack is re-entered mid-way (resumed): 9.5 times a frame in Emerald. A spike sent those resumes to the interpreter: every checkpoint of the new-game route still matched, but compiled share fell from 99.2% to 93.1% and the intro ran 20-60% slower (still far above real time). Design: docs/structured-codegen-design.md, step 5.

options.label: One structured body; resumes interpreted, then won back
options.changes: No code growth. Share drops ~6 points until two runtime units land before your review: calls that don't unwind and IRQs taken inside the tick

options.label: Two bodies: structured from the entry, v1 for resumes
options.changes: No share drop and no runtime change, but every function's generated code roughly doubles (build time and memory up, against phase 1)

options.label: One structured body; resumes interpreted, won back later
options.changes: As a, but the two runtime units move after your review, so you'd review with the ~6-point drop

answer.note: One body, but the runtime changes come first and change: calls settled in place (wider), IRQs in the tick, and the guest on its own stack so the frame end doesn't unwind. Spike: 1 resume a frame, 99.2% compiled, hashes exact. Design doc steps 5-8.

questions.title: How should a headless lane get SSH onto your Deck?
questions.context: You OK'd a 1-minute Emerald benchmark on the Deck for {unit:multiplayer/deck-frame-cost}. The Deck is awake on the tailnet (tailscale ping answers), but ssh deck@steamdeck from quack stops at 'Tailscale SSH requires an additional check: visit login.tailscale.com/a/…': the tailnet's SSH rule for the Deck is in check mode, which wants a browser login every so often. A headless lane can't click that, so the benchmark can't run. (ssh to the name 'steamdeck' also says 'no route to host' on port 22; the tailnet IP the Deck's tailnet address reaches Tailscale SSH.)

options.label: Switch the Deck's SSH rule to accept
options.changes: In the tailnet ACL, set the ssh rule that lets your machines reach deck@steamdeck to action 'accept' instead of 'check'. Lanes then reach the Deck with no login; the next session runs the benchmark straight away.

options.label: You approve the check now and then
options.changes: Leave check mode; you open the login link from a quack terminal (ssh deck@steamdeck once) shortly before a lane runs the unit; it works for the check period (12 h by default). The unit stays blocked until you say you did.

options.label: Skip the Deck measurement
options.changes: Drop the unit; docs/research/multiplayer.md keeps its 2-2.5x-slower estimate for the Deck.

answer.note: june 2026-10-27: lanes can already ssh onto the Deck via Tailscale, but must ask june before each time they do; june approves, then the unit runs.

questions.title: Registers in Rust locals cost 58% more build for no speed: keep, drop or turn on?
questions.context: Step 9 of docs/structured-codegen-design.md, spiked on Emerald (numbers in that step). Locals are exact (sst-gen 0 differ, same new-game frame hash, fn-diff 0 of 6,380 runs differ) but part p07 builds in 38 s instead of 24 s, at 1.4 GB instead of 0.76 GB, its object is 46% bigger, the whole build no longer fits 6 jobs in 8 GB, and LLVM crashes on part p37 unless it is built at opt-level s. The new-game route ran no faster (2.6-3.5 s against 2.6-3.2 s for 5,400 frames). As the card says, I stopped and am reporting. The code is on the branch, off by default, so generated code is unchanged.

options.label: Keep it, off
options.changes: The locals printer and its write-back check stay behind gbaa-recompile --locals and fn-diff's locals form; nothing generated changes; {unit:structured/regs-locals} is recorded done as a stopped spike and the before-more-ROMs look can start

options.label: Drop the code
options.changes: Same generated code; codegen loses the locals module and its check (about 700 lines); the measurements stay in the design doc; the unit is dropped and the look can start

options.label: Turn it on anyway
options.changes: Every Emerald-size build about 1.6x slower and 1.9x the memory, with an opt-level workaround for the LLVM crash; this unit then still owes all routes, CPU suites and own-state-check with locals before the look

options.label: Try a cheaper form first
options.changes: A new unit spikes locals only in functions with no tick inside a loop (or only hot ones); the look waits for it

answer.note: june 2026-10-26: keep it, off by default behind --locals. It's the play view's answer; a future mod view may turn it on per function.

questions.title: May readable Rust leave dead scratch registers at a return?
questions.context: The readable-form spike wrote 8 Emerald functions as Rust near pret's C, exact. About a third of each body is syncing r1-r3, r12 and the flags at each return and tick, values no C caller reads. Today 'exact' means the full machine state matches the generated code's, so they must stay. docs/mod-view-design.md, 'How close exact Rust gets to pret's C', gap 1.

options.label: Keep full-state exactness; move the syncs out of the body
options.changes: Each function gets its return syncs in a macro at its top or a trailing block, so the body reads like C. fn-diff stays the bar. The default.

options.label: Allow registers dead at every return site to differ
options.changes: The printer drops those syncs, so bodies get about a third shorter. Needs an interprocedural liveness proof, and fn-diff compares only live state at returns. The Emerald route same-states check still runs.

questions.title: Where should a game's saves, states and resume file live?
questions.context: Today the .sav, the four .stateN slots and the .resume auto state all sit beside the ROM (ROM.sav etc.), settings.conf in ~/.config/gbaa. Launchers like ES-DE keep ROMs in their own folders, so switching launchers or moving ROMs can strand a save. The frontend unit adds --save-dir/--state-dir/--config-dir flags whatever you pick; this is about the default when no flag is given.

options.label: One home per game under the data dir, keyed by ROM hash
options.changes: Default becomes $XDG_DATA_HOME/gbaa/games/<rom-hash>/ (save, states, resume, backups); a save found beside the ROM is picked up once (moved in, original kept as .sav.bak) so nothing is shadowed. Moving or renaming the ROM never loses progress.

options.label: Keep everything beside the ROM
options.changes: No change to defaults; only the new flags. Matches mGBA/RetroArch-from-folder habits and stays portable on SD cards, but moving the ROM leaves its save behind.

options.label: Hash home, but keep the .sav beside the ROM if one exists there
options.changes: New games go to the per-hash home; a game already with ROM.sav keeps using it in place (never moved), states and resume go to the hash home. Nothing on disk is touched, at the cost of two places to look.

answer.note: Per-game folder under a readable name (build's name, set at recompile; interpreter slugs the file name), not a hash. Order: --save-dir/--state-dir (exact folder) > per-game menu setting > global setting > <OS data dir>/gbaa/saves/<name>/. Files named after the game. States/resume record the ROM hash, load anyway with a .bak on mismatch, research whether that's risky. Old saves beside the ROM copied in once, originals kept. Full design: docs/save-locations-design.md

questions.title: May the native port's check use a new timing, not exact?
questions.context: A native port (a game as a plain Rust program) counts no cycles: its time moves only when the game waits for V-blank, spins in a loop, or reads the beam or a timer. The play build at exact timing lags and takes interrupts mid-frame where the native program can't, so they part ways at the first lag frame (Emerald's intro has one). docs/native-port-design.md, section 7. Today's rule says every check passes --timing exact.

options.label: Add --timing native for the native check
options.changes: the play build and interpreter get a fourth timing that moves the clock where the native program does; the native check compares frames and RAM byte for byte against that build, every frame. mGBA stays the oracle for the play build through its exact checks, as now. One more timing to keep correct ({unit:native/timing-native})

options.label: Native check against exact only
options.changes: no new timing; the native check compares by game frame and only up to the first lag frame or mid-frame interrupt, replaying timer reads; long routes can't be checked exactly

questions.title: How should a busy loop that calls functions let time pass under native timing?
questions.context: Found by {unit:native/timing-native}: Emerald hangs under --timing native at the new game's map load. DoMapLoadLoop spins until the V-blank handler drains the DMA3 queue, polling through function calls. The design only lets time pass at store-free, call-free loops, so time never moves and V-blank never comes. A native program lifted from the same code would hang the same way, so the native check and the Stage-A lifter both wait on this. The timing itself is built on branch t3/c58bf1ab (head f773f153): unit tests pass, 8 of 15 agb programs match compiled vs interpreted.

options.label: Back-edge budget
options.changes: both builds count backward branches; after ~10,000 with no time passing, the next one counts as an idle loop. Deterministic, same instruction in both builds, works for any game. Cost: the native program carries a counting call on loop back edges the analysis can't prove finish, a little less plain than hand-written Rust

options.label: Widen idle through calls
options.changes: a loop counts as idle if the functions it calls don't store, using the new function summaries. Native code stays clean, but fragile: LoadMapInStepsLocal does store in other states, so Emerald's loop may still not qualify

options.label: Hand-mark wait loops per game
options.changes: a list of known wait loops per game in TOML. Cheapest and cleanest output, but every new game needs hand work and an unlisted loop hangs

answer.note: june 2026-11-01: default to (a), refined per docs/research/busy-wait-loops.md: count only loops that contain a call, each loop on its own; past ~2,000 passes with no time passing, each pass moves the clock half a scanline (hw::spin in native code), under --timing native only. Also build the tooling for (c): a per-game list of wait loops (TOML) as a fallback for loops the rule misses, with the hole report flagging candidates.
